r31.argument: A reader might feel the council is cast unfavorably: 'several council members cited it in their remarks before the vote' and 'a single chart nearly closed three branch libraries.' But the writer never blames the council; the villain is the chart and the luck of 'who happens to be in the room.' Option [2] is directly contradicted by 'He was not an expert.'

Option [3] echoes the real claim of ¶5 ('A picture that persuades in two seconds also deceives in two seconds'), but ¶3's numbers are explicitly introduced by 'The need is not speculative' and concluded by 'Five minutes moved the needle,' which match the key. No alternative has a genuine case.

The writer does grant a point as fair and does narrow to 'a four-week unit,' but that is the response to 'The concern about time,' not overlap; for overlap the writer says the concern 'is, we think, mistaken' and distinguishes building from evaluating. Only a reader who conflates the two concerns would pick [1].

One could note ¶3 does add specificity ('1,140 students across four district high schools'), but it is evidence, not 'scheduling details,' and does not restate the recommendation. Option [1] fails because ¶3 does not 'challenge' ¶2. Key is clearly correct.

'hiding something under the sauce' does connote deliberate concealment, and the preceding sentence mentions someone who 'chosen the frame with care.' But the writer also says 'a well-made chart can tell the truth faster than a paragraph can' and does not claim 'most' producers deceive. The key's phrase 'settle the overlap objection' is slightly strong (writer says only 'is, we think, mistaken'), but the analogy's function is plainly to make the build/judge distinction concrete.
r31.key_flaw: Justification says the analogy 'clinches' the rebuttal; the passage frames it as illustrative ('The difference is the difference between...'), so 'settle' is a mild overstatement but not a substantive error.

r31.argument: A reader might think the contrast implies math instruction is inadequate and should 'give way,' but the writer concedes math classes 'teach students to build charts correctly' and proposes the unit live in 'civics or English,' not that math yield. The stem's description 'two balanced clauses' is slightly loose since the second clause is much longer ('or built it correctly and chosen the frame with care'), but the parallel subject-verb-object opening is real.
r31.stem_issue: The clauses are parallel in opening structure but not strictly 'balanced' in length; minor imprecision, does not affect the answer.

r32.argument: A reader fixated on paragraph 3 might argue the essay responds to media-driven alarm: the Courier 'ran the story under a headline that called the bees "a swarm of menace"' and 'Within a month the council passed an ordinance.' But that campaign is a 1923 historical episode, not the occasion of the essay; the framing in ¶1 and ¶6 is unmistakably the councilman's remark at the Castellanos hearing ('So when the councilman says bees do not belong in a modern city, I want to hand him the ledger'). Option [1] is factually contradicted ('The ordinance was repealed in 1981'), and [3] misreads the ledger as a new discovery.

The nineteen households are explicitly reused in paragraph 3 as the baseline for the ban's effect: 'within a year the nineteen households had become none. Nothing had changed about the bees.' So the count does help support the claim that the ban reflected the city's self-image rather than any change in bee behavior. However, in its paragraph-2 context the figure is introduced to document growth of a shared urban history ('The bees, in other words, did not merely tolerate the city; they ate it'), directly answering ¶1's 'They have shared a great many, and most of them were written in Halverton.' The 'primarily' in the stem keeps [3] the better answer.

'The ban was less a response to danger than a tidying away of the past' is the passage's sharpest interpretive thesis about the historical episode, and ¶4 and ¶6 both build on it ('not relics of a slower century'). A reader could argue the essay's real argument is about why the ban happened, not about chronological belonging. But that sentence governs only the 1923 episode; the keyed sentence in ¶6 directly rebuts the councilman's claim that frames and closes the essay. One could note the essay's culminating claim ('a city is not only pavement and ordinance but a living thing... They are the ones who keep it alive') is arguably more central than the keyed sentence, but it is not offered as an option.

A partial reader stopping at the opening of ¶4 might take 'I do not want to pretend the worries were all invented... his mother's anger was neither foolish nor small' as a retraction of ¶3's claim that the ban was mere 'tidying away.' But the paragraph immediately pivots with 'But a city that outlawed every creature capable of causing two days in bed would have to begin with its horses,' and reframes: 'The question was never whether bees could do harm. The question was whether the harm was large enough.' That is concession-then-reframing, not withdrawal. [2] is wrong because ¶4 stays in 1923; the jump to 1974 is ¶5.

Paragraph 5 does bring the historical narrative to its chronological close ('Today the archive holds photographs of hives on the library roof...'), so the first half of [3] is accurate. But the 'final judgment on the councilman's assertion' is delivered in ¶6 ('So when the councilman says... I want to hand him the ledger'), not ¶5. The key's reading—revival 'the way weeds come back to a vacant lot' undercutting the 'thing left over from a slower century' framing—is well supported. [1] misreads the inspectors, who 'could not bring themselves to write him up,' and [2] invents a personal beekeeping experience the writer never claims.

The only textual hook for [1] is 'a measure of patience with the occasional sting,' which a careless reader might call a 'hazard.' But the sentence lists 'a roof, a water dish' as modest asks, not hazards, and the return is 'a reminder that a city is... a living thing,' not honey. Options [2] and [3] contradict the explicit asymmetry ('What they ask of us is small'). No reasonable expert would choose any alternative.

w31.argument: Option 0 does return to the council and the pending decision ("Perhaps the council could keep half of the block quiet"), so it partially meets the 'returns to the upcoming vote' half of the goal. But it proposes a compromise rather than urging that the block be kept "as it is," directly contradicting the stated goal and the title "Leave Tuesday Empty." Option 3 explicitly names "When the council votes next month" (echoing sentence 3, "Next month the student council will vote") and asks to "leave those twenty-five empty minutes exactly as they are." No expert would choose 0.

Option 1 is unquestionably respectful ("Council members surely know best"), but it abandons the writer's position entirely ("I will trust whatever schedule they decide on"), failing the 'still holding firm against the proposal' requirement. Options 0 and 2 are disrespectful or overgeneralized ("Every single student... agrees with me"; "the council has never had an original thought"). Option 3 is the only one that is both courteous ("I ask council members to weigh...") and opposed ("before trading the week's only unscheduled stretch for one more schedule"). Key is sound.

Option 0 does take a clear, arguable position ("The council should keep the quiet block") and gives two reasons, so a careless reader who stops at 'arguable thesis with two reasons' might choose it. However, its reasons—"enrichment sessions would cost money and require extra teacher training"—appear nowhere in the editorial; paragraph 2 is about student work (sentences 5-7) and paragraph 3 answers critics about sleeping and doodling (sentences 8-10). Option 1's "boredom has sparked real student work" and "even its idle moments have value" map exactly onto those paragraphs.

Option 1 is the only distractor that refers to both examples ("Both of us") and plausibly fits chronologically after sentence 7, so a partial reader might take it as tying the two together. But it merely explains why the students had free time ("our assignments that week turned out to be short") rather than explaining how the examples support the claim that boredom leads to meaningful work; it even slightly undercuts the point by implying homework would otherwise have filled the block. Option 2 explicitly does the analytic work: "having no assignment was not an obstacle; it was the reason our minds wandered toward something worth making."
w31.stem_issue: The stem refers to 'the claim that unstructured boredom leads to meaningful work' as though stated in the passage; it is implied by sentences 5-7 and 10 but never explicitly stated. Minor, since the intended claim is clear.

w31.argument: Option 0 is a comparison involving idleness ("A runner who skips every practice"), but it argues the opposite point—that idleness harms later performance ("likely to finish far behind")—which would support the critics in sentence 8 ("unstructured time is wasted time") rather than the writer. Option 3 likewise condemns apparent idleness ("being rude to a teacher"). Option 2 is etymology, not a comparison. Only option 1's fallow field ("not wasting it; she is letting the soil recover for the next harvest") shows seeming idleness enabling later work, directly rebutting sentence 8 and extending sentence 10.

Option 3 preserves the original meaning faithfully ("students can think about things they themselves choose" retains the self-chosen emphasis of "in a way that they choose themselves without being told what to think about") and is grammatically complete, so it is a legitimate revision. But it retains the wordy frame "is a period of time in which," which is exactly the redundancy the stem asks to eliminate; option 2 says the same thing in fewer words ("gives students time to think about whatever they choose"). Option 0 changes the meaning to "schoolwork," and option 1 is a fragment. Key is correct; 3 is a second-best, not an equal.

w32.argument: Option [1] ("Radio has changed a great deal in forty years...") at least echoes the essay's forty-year frame from sentence 2 and could serve as a generic closer, but it neither urges readers to donate nor returns to the "know what I like / know where I live" contrast of sentence 4. Option [2] actually reverses the writer's thesis, and [3] is a tribute, not a call to pledge. The key ("pledge to the one station that knows where you live") uniquely satisfies both stated criteria.

Option [3] ("A few people ... may have had their radios turned on") does remove the overstatement, but it swings to understatement and fails the second half of the goal, which requires the sentence to "still suggest how widely the broadcast was heard." Option [2] keeps the absolute ("without exception"), and [0] changes the subject to podcasts. The key's "hundreds of households" with the hedge "Judging by the calls the station logged" is the only option satisfying both criteria. Minor note: the key introduces evidence (call logs) not present in the passage, though this is standard for revision items.

Option [3] does "acknowledge what streaming services do well," but it goes far beyond acknowledgment, asserting algorithms are "better than radio in nearly every way, including during floods," which directly contradicts the paragraph's evidence (sentence 5: "it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed"). Option [0] concedes nothing; [2] is an irrelevant fact. The key's concession-plus-reassertion structure, tied to the "dry cots" detail of sentence 5, is clearly best.

Option [3] is the only distractor offering a specific, concrete detail ("The transmitter ... was installed when the station first went on the air"), and it connects to sentence 2, but it illustrates the station's age and need, not that "ordinary people keep it going." Option [0] merely restates the claim, and [1] generalizes away from Riverbend. The key's roofer and bakery example is the only one that is both specific and on-claim.

Option [3] ("Fiscal resources allocated to the station remain suboptimal...") removes the flippant "pathetic" and "kind of a joke" and is at least respectful, so a reader focused only on eliminating sarcasm might pick it. But it is bureaucratic jargon, not "sincere, admiring," and it doesn't set up the pivot "Yet it does survive." Option [0] keeps the mocking tone; [2] contradicts sentence 12 and the pledge appeal. The key's "close to remarkable" is admiring and uses a passage detail (the marching band).

Option [0] ("midnight Sunday, because a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air") does eliminate the comma splice and is grammatically acceptable as a main clause plus subordinate clause. However, the stem asks for a revision that "correctly joins the two independent clauses"; subordinating the second clause with "because" means it is no longer independent, and it also creates an illogical causal relationship (the drive's hours are not caused by the value of a donation). Option [1] creates a run-on and [2] misuses commas around "and." The semicolon in the key is the clean fix.
